meta.subtitle: Half-year GAAP profit and a sharp rise in free cash flow, set against revenue that lags volume and a concentrated customer base

advisories: model vs Street expected return diverge by 44pp — informational, not scored

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate Marqeta HOLD with a $15 to $21 target range. The 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 shows a business growing revenue in the high teens and earning a GAAP net profit over the six months ended June 30, 2026, and free cash flow rose sharply in FY25. Two things keep us from buying. Processing volume is growing faster than revenue, which we think partly reflects how Revenue Share is priced. And a small number of customers, Block among them, carry significant revenue; Block has already obtained reduced pricing once, so a renegotiation is a demonstrated risk rather than a hypothetical one. Against that, cash generation and a balance sheet that shows no debt limit how far a reasonable bear case can go. The scenarios derive HOLD on the page's rule, and we have not shaded the call in either direction.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Marqeta, Inc. runs a cloud-based open API platform for card issuing and transaction processing; it was incorporated in 2010 and is headquartered in Oakland, California. Per the 10-Q MD&A, every customer takes issuer processor services as the core offering, and customers can add Bank and Network Management, Program Management (chargebacks and dispute resolution, reconciliation and card fulfillment) and Value Added Services such as tokenization, real-time decisioning and fraud management. The company reports a single reportable segment. Verticals named in the company description include financial services, on-demand services, lending, expense management, e-commerce enablement and buy now, pay later providers.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: Marqeta earned a GAAP net profit in the six months ended June 30, 2026 while growing revenue in the high teens, and its free cash flow rose sharply in FY25. The shares trade near the low end of the 52-week range and below every Street target, yet most analysts rate them Hold. Upside needs revenue growth to run ahead of a consensus path that already assumes deceleration, while operating costs stay contained. The widening gap between processing volume and revenue is the main risk to that path, and dependence on Block and a few other large customers is the second. We think risk and reward are roughly balanced at $16.55.

catalysts: A GAAP operating profit for full-year 2026; the six months ended June 30, 2026 were profitable at the net income line, and the Financials section sets out how.
Revenue growth that holds near the Q2'26 pace instead of slowing to the FY26E consensus; see Growth.
Disclosure in a future filing of Block terms that preserve pricing; the pack gives no renewal date, and the Risks section explains why it matters.
Repurchases paced to free cash flow rather than drawn from the cash balance; see Capital allocation.
risks: Customer concentration, with Block named among a small number of significant customers; see Risks.
Revenue growth lagging volume as Revenue Share rates rise with customer volume; see Growth.
A cash balance and current ratio well below earlier years; see the balance sheet commentary.
Dual class voting that leaves outside holders little leverage; see Governance.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Profitability turned in 2026. The 10-Q MD&A reports net income of $15,401 thousand for the six months ended June 30, 2026, against a loss of $8,907 thousand a year earlier, with Q2'26 contributing $7,567 thousand. Gross margin was 69% in both second quarters, so the better operating result came from expenses: total operating expenses rose to $118,237 thousand from $113,289 thousand, far more slowly than the revenue growth set out under Growth, and the Q2'26 operating margin was 2.1%. Adjusted EBITDA margin, a non-GAAP measure, rose to 21% from 19% in the quarter. The trailing figures still lag, with a TTM operating margin of -1.9% and a net loss of $13.9M for FY25, so a profitable half does not yet make a profitable year. The annual series needs care. The 10-K risk factors attribute the FY24 revenue decrease primarily to the August 2023 Block Amendment, which allowed reduced pricing and, from July 1, 2023, moved Cash App fees owed to Issuing Banks and Card Networks out of costs of revenue and into a reduction of net revenue. Moving a cost out of costs of revenue and into a revenue reduction lifts gross margin mechanically, so we read much of the step from 48.7% in FY23 to 69.4% in FY24 as presentation; the 10-K does not make that link itself. The earnings improvement is real, but it rests on cost discipline that has to persist while revenue growth slows.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: Cash and short-term investments stood at $0.7B at FY25, down from $1.2B in FY21 and FY22. Total equity fell from $1.6B in FY21 to $0.8B in FY25, and the current ratio dropped to 1.65 in FY25 from 3.37 a year earlier; the TTM reading is 1.66. The Total Debt and Net Debt rows are blank, no interest coverage is shown, and the MD&A describes other income as mainly interest income, so we treat the company as carrying little or no borrowing, though the pack states no debt figure. The facts do not break out current liabilities, so we cannot say what drove the current ratio's decline beyond the fall in cash. The capital allocation discussion under Management explains where the cash went. The balance sheet remains sound, but it is no longer the excess-capital position it was in FY21.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation stepped up in FY25. Operating cash flow reached $0.2B, capital expenditure was $30.3M and free cash flow was $132.4M, an FCF margin of 21.2% against 7.3% in FY24 and well above any earlier year shown. Capital expenditure is the difference between the two cash lines, so free cash flow is the better measure of what the business can return. The FCF margin sits far above the FY25 operating margin of -7.4%. The MD&A's Adjusted EBITDA definition adds back depreciation and amortization and share-based compensation, non-cash items that also separate operating income from operating cash flow, but the facts size neither of them, nor working capital, so we cannot say how much of the gap each explains. That makes FY25 one strong year rather than an established level; the Valuation section notes trailing evidence that cash generation continued into 2026. How the cash was spent is judged under Capital allocation.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: On earnings the stock looks expensive and on cash it looks inexpensive. Trailing P/E is 183.9x and EV/EBITDA is 62.9x because trailing GAAP earnings are barely positive. The forward P/E the vendor labels NTM, 61.3x, equals the price over FY26E consensus EPS of $0.27, so we read it as a current-year multiple; on FY27E consensus EPS of $0.50 the multiple is ~33.1x. The vendor does not say whether these estimates are GAAP or adjusted, so we do not treat the forward multiples as GAAP-based. P/S is 2.5x, and the page does not label its revenue window. The TTM FCF yield is 9.7%, higher than FY25 free cash flow alone would give against a ~$1.7B market cap, which suggests trailing free cash flow ran above the FY25 level; the pack has no quarterly cash flow statement to confirm it. One caveat applies to every market-value figure: the Quote derives ~104.1M shares from the market cap, while the proxy reports 392,067,528 Class A and 32,808,210 Class B shares outstanding as of April 15, 2026. The sources do not explain the difference. We use the vendor figures as given, but on the proxy count the FCF yield would be lower and P/S higher than shown. The Street is cautious: 14 analysts split 3 Buy, 10 Hold and 1 Sell, with a consensus target of $20.50, a median of $19.50 and a range of $17.00 to $28.00.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Revenue growth holds near the Q2'26 pace instead of slowing to consensus, operating costs stay contained, and earnings reach the FY27E consensus. We value the shares at 46x FY27E consensus EPS, a premium to today's FY27E multiple for growth that holds up but still below today's current-year multiple; that sits between the consensus target and the Street high.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Revenue lands near the FY26E consensus as growth slows, and earnings follow the consensus path. We value the shares at 36x FY27E consensus EPS, a little above today's FY27E multiple because those earnings are a year nearer, and far below today's current-year multiple because growth is slowing; that sits between the Street's low and median targets.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Block reprices or Revenue Share step-ups stall revenue growth, and operating results return to a loss like FY25's. We value the shares at two times FY25 revenue of $624.9M on the vendor share count, below today's P/S because revenue stops growing; that is below the 52-week low of $14.80.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: The weights rest on different evidence from the multiples. Bear carries 30% because the downside has precedent: the 10-K ties the FY24 revenue decrease primarily to the August 2023 Block Amendment, it still names Block among a small number of significant customers, and Revenue Share rates rise as customers' volumes grow, a mechanism consistent with TPV outgrowing revenue (see Growth). Bull carries 25% because it needs two things at once: growth above a consensus path that already assumes deceleration, and costs that stay contained. The cost performance in the six months ended June 30, 2026 supports the second condition but says nothing about growth. Base carries 45% because revenue for the six months ended June 30, 2026 leaves the FY26 consensus within reach (see Growth). On these weights the probability-weighted value is $17.45, expected upside is +5.4%, bear-case downside is -27.5% and reward/risk is 0.20×, which derives HOLD. The call is not close to either line: swapping the Bull and Bear weights still derives HOLD, and so does any Base multiple from today's FY27E multiple up to one that matches the Street median target. We do not set the Bear lower because the cash generation and blank debt rows set out under Financials do not depend on the disputed share count. Our weighted value sits below the Street median target because of the Bear weight; that is a judgment about Block, not a finding.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Marqeta reports a single reportable segment, so no product or geographic revenue split is available. The 10-Q MD&A divides net revenue into platform services revenue, net, which carries Interchange Fees net of Revenue Share plus processing and other fees, and other services revenue, mainly card fulfillment, without sizing them in the excerpt. The economics turn on the platform line, where what the company pays customers in Revenue Share and what it earns in Card Network incentives both move with volume.

moatFactors.name: Embedded infrastructure and switching costs
moatFactors.body: Per the 10-Q MD&A, customers can embed Marqeta without having to build certain complex compliance elements or customer support services, and the company can connect them to an Issuing Bank partner as BIN sponsor and manage compliance with Card Network rules. In our view that makes a working card program costly to move. Switching costs did not, however, stop Block from obtaining reduced pricing, as set out under Risks.

moatFactors.name: Volume-based network incentives
moatFactors.body: The 10-Q MD&A says Card Network incentives reach a higher cumulative rate as processing volumes increase, which rewards scale in costs of revenue in arrangements where the company acts as principal. The Revenue Share step-up described under Growth works in the other direction, so scale raises what the company pays customers as well as what it earns from networks.

moatFactors.name: Customer concentration
moatFactors.body: Pricing power with the big customers is the weak point. The concentration set out under Risks means an advantage built on embedded infrastructure is still renegotiated customer by customer.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat NARROW. The embedded services hold customers on the platform, and the TPV growth under Growth suggests the platform keeps winning volume. The pricing history cuts the other way: the Block Amendment and the volume-linked Revenue Share mean scale has not turned into pricing power with the big accounts. The 10-K risk factors also describe markets that are competitive and continuously evolving, without naming rivals in the excerpt. The advantage looks durable enough to keep customers, but not strong enough to hold price with the accounts that carry concentration risk.

points: Volume is growing quickly. The 10-Q MD&A reports Q2'26 TPV of $120,423 million against $91,386 million a year earlier, and the 10-K risk factors report FY25 TPV of $382.5 billion, up 31%.

Revenue is growing more slowly than volume. Q2'26 revenue rose 17%, well below that quarter's TPV growth, and in FY25 revenue growth of +23.3% trailed TPV growth. The 10-Q MD&A says that, generally, as customers' processing volumes increase, the rates at which the company shares revenue with them increase, and that Revenue Share is recorded as a reduction to net revenue. We think that is one reason revenue lags TPV, though the filing does not say so or quantify it.

Consensus expects deceleration, with FY26E revenue of ~$704M (+13%) and FY27E revenue of $807.2M. The 10-Q MD&A supports the FY26 figure: six-month net revenue of $341,793 thousand against $289,465 thousand leaves the second half needing growth well below the pace of the year to date to reach consensus.

The 10-K risk factors list acceptance in markets outside the United States, new offerings and a more diversified customer base among the factors future revenue growth depends on. None is quantified in the facts, so we give them no weight in the Base case.

Against that, the slowdown is already in the numbers: Q2'26 growth is below FY25's pace, and consensus expects a further step down for FY26. If the gap with TPV widens, growth could fall below the Street's path.

management.leadership: The proxy statement dated April 21, 2026 lists Mike Milotich, Patti Kangwangkij, Todd Pollak and Crystal Sumner in its beneficial-ownership table under the heading for named executive officers, directors and director nominees; the excerpt gives none of their titles. The same proxy identifies Simon Khalaf as the former Chief Executive Officer and refers to a former Executive Chairman without naming that person in the excerpt. Leadership has therefore changed at the top, but the excerpt does not date Mr. Khalaf's separation, give a reason for it or name a successor. We cannot judge the current team on a history the sources do not provide; the cost discipline in the 2026 results, set out under Financials, is the clearest evidence available on execution.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation has leaned heavily toward buybacks. Share repurchases rose from $0.1B in FY22 to $0.4B in FY25, well above the FY25 free cash flow set out under Financials, and that gap is the main reason cash and short-term investments fell in FY25 despite a strong cash year. The company pays no dividend. The 10-K risk factors say the company cannot guarantee that its share repurchase program will enhance long-term stockholder value and that repurchases may reduce working capital. Repurchasing at today's price is defensible given the cash the business generates, but the FY25 pace drew down the buffer, and a pace closer to free cash flow would be the more prudent course while Block's pricing and the Revenue Share drift remain open questions.
management.governance: Per the proxy statement dated April 21, 2026, the Board determined that eight directors are independent under Nasdaq standards: Mmes. Atkinson, Cummings, Paul and Thomas and Messrs. Chokshi, Graf, Linville and Prasad. Jud Linville has served as independent Board Chair since June 2024, and the proxy cites his past experience as Chief Executive Officer of Global Cards and Consumer Services at Citigroup Inc. The structure that matters most for outside holders is the dual class. The 10-K risk factors state that it has the effect of concentrating voting control with Class B holders, including directors, executive officers and their affiliates, and that the Class A trading price may be depressed as a result. An independent chair and an independent board majority provide oversight, but Class A holders' ability to shape contested decisions is limited, as the ownership figures below show.
management.insiderOwnership: As of April 15, 2026, per the proxy, Jason Gardner held 94.99% of the Class B common stock and 46.92% of total voting power, and all directors and executive officers as a group held 48.62% of total voting power. The excerpt does not state Mr. Gardner's current role. Neither holding is a majority, so this is not control, but Mr. Gardner alone sits close to one, and outside holders would have to vote largely together to outvote him on a contested matter. Other 5% holders listed include entities associated with T. Rowe Price Associates at 7.81% and T. Rowe Price Investment Management at 4.21% of voting power, and entities associated with BlackRock, Inc. at 3.92%; the Vanguard row carries no figures in the excerpt. For Class A investors, that means limited practical leverage on contested matters.

idiosyncratic: Block concentration: the 10-K risk factors state that the company generates significant net revenue from a small number of customers, including Block, and that the loss of any of these relationships, or renewals on less favorable terms, could adversely affect results. The August 2023 Block Amendment allowed reduced pricing, so this risk has already played out once. The pack gives no renewal date for Block, so the sources do not let us time the next negotiation.

Take-rate compression: if volume growth concentrates in large customers, the Revenue Share step-up described under Growth could keep revenue growth lagging TPV. The quarterly gap between TPV growth and revenue growth is the measure that would show it.

Bank and network dependence: the 10-K risk factors state that the company relies on its relationships with Issuing Banks and Card Networks, and the 10-Q MD&A says network incentives are subject to cumulative volume thresholds within an annual measurement period that, for certain arrangements, may not align with the fiscal year. A missed threshold could raise costs of revenue in arrangements where the company acts as principal and pull gross margin below the levels set out under Financials. The sources show no sign of a change in partners.
risks.systemic: The 10-Q MD&A states that management is unable to predict how macroeconomic factors, including geopolitical conflicts, changes in inflation and interest rates and uncertainty from potential tariffs, will affect processing volumes, and that a deterioration could increase the risk of lower consumer spending. Because revenue is tied to Interchange Fees and processing fees, weaker spending could reach revenue quickly. Regulation is a second channel: the 10-K risk factors note that rules applying directly and through Issuing Banks and Card Networks are subject to change and uncertain interpretation. Interest rates matter in a smaller way, because other income consists primarily of interest income from short-term investments and cash deposits, and that income shrinks as cash is spent or as rates fall. We see these risks as cyclical rather than thesis-breaking, but they would amplify a Bear case driven by customer pricing.

body: HOLD, target range $15 to $21. GAAP profit in the six months ended June 30, 2026, high-teens revenue growth and the FY25 step-up in free cash flow are why we do not rate the shares below HOLD. We stop short of BUY because volume growth is not fully reaching revenue and Block has already obtained reduced pricing once; the Bear weight that follows from those two facts keeps the expected upside short of the BUY line.

Because the Bear sits well below the price, a BUY needs either a lower share price or much less Bear weight. On the current scenarios, the label turns BUY on a fall that stops short of the 52-week low of $14.80, and SELL on a rise that stops short of the Street median target of $19.50. On fundamentals, we would cut the Bear weight on a full-year 2026 GAAP operating profit with revenue growth holding near the Q2'26 pace, or on disclosed Block terms that preserve pricing, and raise it on a Block amendment that cuts pricing.
